Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Vignette:
The explosion happened on a Tuesday in the central plaza of her hometown, just two days after her thirty-second birthday. Clara, a forty-four-year-old American woman of Guatemalan and Cuban descent, had been buying flowers for her mother’s altar when the first charge detonated near the fountain, followed seconds later by a second blast near the market stalls. The force threw her against a stone pillar, and a jagged piece of masonry caught her left thigh, tearing through her skirt and leaving a hot, bleeding wound she couldn’t stop pressing with her hands. She watched people fall around her, the air thick with dust and the copper taste of blood. She survived, but the plaza was left in ruins. In the months that followed, Clara went over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, tracing the timing of the blasts and the faces in the crowd until the sequence blurred. The memories refused to sit neatly in the past. When they surfaced, they arrived all at once, completely real across all her senses: the searing heat on her skin, the deafening roar, the grit of concrete in her mouth, the sight of her own blood pooling on the cobblestones. Yet when she tried to deliberately remember what happened, she found it difficult to access the memory. The words would catch in her throat, the narrative fractured into fragments that refused to hold together. Physical pain in that same leg soon arrived alongside a heavy wave of fear, horror, guilt, and shame. She learned to scan every doorway, every window, before letting herself settle. In the sacristy, the convent kitchen, and the parish hall, her eyes would dart to the nearest exit, always identifying escape routes before she could feel comfortable anywhere. Crowds grew impossible. The idea of standing in a supermarket aisle or walking through a packed weekend mass made her chest tighten until she turned back, choosing instead to walk long distances alone to avoid crowded places. When nightmares came, they pulled her out of bed gasping, the dream residue lingering in her limbs for hours, leaving her certain that the danger was still unfolding. The most terrifying moments arrived without warning. She would be arranging hymnals and suddenly the memory would force its way into her mind when she did not want it to, as vivid and suffocating as if the air were still filling with smoke. She would have to step into the chapel’s side alcove, pressing her palms to her face until the sensation passed. As a nun, Clara’s life was built on presence, yet her divorce had settled years ago, leaving her with a quiet routine dedicated to the habit and the schedule. She found herself avoiding intimacy, keeping her hands tucked close to her body and refusing to sit across from anyone in conversation. She had come to believe that leaning into another person’s confidence would only leave her exposed to sudden loss. Her only reliable sanctuary became her small cell and the space behind the main altar during silent hours. Outside those boundaries, the ground felt unstable. The liturgical elements that once brought her peace now posed a quiet threat; a drop of wine on a chalice cloth or a drop of blood from a paper cut on her finger triggered a physical stillness so complete she had to step outside and wait for her breathing to slow. For years, she managed by shrinking her world to the safe perimeters she could control, trading the demands of community for the rigid geometry of her routine. But lately, the exhaustion had outpaced her vigilance. The pain in her leg no longer needed to be sharp to alarm her; the ghost of it was enough. She found herself sitting in the chapel after Compline, hands folded but heart racing, wondering how long she could keep translating survival into silence. She came to the clinic because the weight of her own mind had grown heavier than her vows. She hoped, more than anything, to find a way to sit in a room without mapping the exits, to let a memory pass through without dragging the room down with it, and perhaps, to touch another person’s hand without feeling the cobblestones beneath her palms.
